w:r.w:t: In the contemporary global landscape of higher education, the university is no longer perceived merely as a center for academic instruction and theoretical research. Instead, modern tertiary institutions are increasingly viewed as holistic environments dedicated to the comprehensive development of human capital. Central to this developmental philosophy is the recognition that the physical well-being of the student population is inextricably linked to their academic success and long-term professional productivity. Regular participation in sports and structured physical activities has been empirically linked to improved cardiovascular health, reduced psychological stress, and significantly enhanced cognitive performance (World Health Organization [WHO], 2022). Research in neurobiology suggests that aerobic exercise stimulates the release of brain-derived neurotrophic factors (BDNF), which support memory retention and executive function qualities that are indispensable for students navigating rigorous academic curricula.

Furthermore, the integration of sports into university life serves as a vital tool for social engineering and character building. Engaging in competitive and recreational athletics fosters essential soft skills such as teamwork, leadership, resilience, and time management. In the Nigerian context, the university system has historically placed a high premium on athletic engagement, a commitment most visibly evidenced by the significance of the Nigerian University Games Association (NUGA). Since its inception, NUGA has served not only as a platform for discovering elite athletic talent but also as a critical vehicle for fostering national unity among a diverse student population (Okey & Adeyemi, 2023). Within institutions like the University of Delta, Agbor, sports facilities serve as a hub for student interaction, contributing to a vibrant campus culture that balances intellectual rigor with physical vitality.

However, as the global sports industry enters the era of the Fourth Industrial Revolution (Industry 4.0), a profound technological divide has emerged. In developed regions, the concept of the Smart Campus has moved from theory to standard practice. International institutions now routinely employ sophisticated Internet of Things (IoT) ecosystems, incorporating wearable sensors, biometric monitors, and real-time data analytics to track athlete performance and ensure student safety. These systems provide coaches and health administrators with instantaneous
insights into exertion levels, recovery rates, and potential injury risks, thereby optimizing the athletic output of the student-body.

Conversely, the management of sports within Nigerian tertiary institutions remains largely anchored in manual, paper-based methodologies (Akinyemi, 2024). This reliance on analogue record-keeping creates a significant administrative bottleneck. Manual registers are frequently characterized by data fragmentation, human error, and a total lack of historical continuity. For the sports directorate, this means that tracking a student's athletic progress over a four-year degree is nearly impossible. More critically, the absence of real-time monitoring presents a safety vacuum; during high-intensity training sessions or football matches at the university sports complex, there is currently no automated mechanism to alert medical staff to physical overexertion or sudden health emergencies.

The emergence of affordable, high-speed mobile computing and Global Positioning Systems (GPS) offers a transformative solution to these local challenges. Real-time tracking systems allow for the instantaneous capture and processing of spatial and temporal data, providing a transparent, verifiable, and permanent record of physical activity. According to Bello and Musa (2021), the integration of digital tracking in African sports management could revolutionize how talent is scouted and how student health is monitored, especially in environments where medical and coaching resources may be overstretched. By shifting from reactive, manual reporting to proactive, data-driven monitoring, universities can ensure a higher standard of accountability in their sports

The ubiquity of smartphones among the Nigerian student population presents a unique and cost-effective opportunity for digital transformation. Most modern mobile devices are equipped with sophisticated micro-electromechanical systems (MEMS), including accelerometers, gyroscopes, and high-precision GPS chips capable of tracking location, velocity, and duration of activity with remarkable accuracy. By developing a localized, software-based system that leverages this existing hardware, universities like the University of Delta can implement high-tech sports monitoring without the prohibitive capital expenditure associated with importing specialized wearable equipment.
This research, therefore, focuses on the design and development of a real-time system specifically tailored to the infrastructural and cultural realities of a Nigerian university. The goal

is to move beyond the limitations of traditional sports management by creating a digital ecosystem where student physical activity is accurately recorded, analyzed in real-time, and utilized for the strategic betterment of the campus community. This study represents a critical step toward the realization of a Smart University in Delta State, where technology and wellness converge to support the next generation of Nigerian graduates.

The current framework for monitoring student sports activities in Nigerian universities is plagued by several critical issues that undermine the efficiency of sports departments and the safety of the student body. These problems are outlined as follows:

Currently, the record-keeping process for student participation in sports is largely manual. This leads to frequent errors in data entry and makes it difficult to maintain a long-term history of student engagement. There is also the risk of ghost participation, where records are falsified, leading to a lack of accountability in the use of university sports resources (Oluwatobi, 2023).

High-intensity physical activity carries inherent risks, such as overexertion, dehydration, or sudden cardiac events. In the absence of a real-time tracking system, coaches and medical personnel have no way of monitoring a student’s activity levels as they occur. If a student collapses during a long-distance run or a football match in a remote part of the campus, there is no automated system to trigger an alert, which is a significant safety hazard (Smith & Johnson, 2021).

Nigerian universities are key pipelines for national sports teams. However, the identification of talented athletes is often based on the subjective observation of coaches during specific trials. This method is flawed as it ignores the consistent, long-term performance data that a digital system could provide. Without objective metrics like average speed, stamina over time, and frequency of training, many high-potential athletes remain undiscovered.

Without precise data on when and where students are exercising, the university administration cannot accurately determine the demand for specific facilities. This leads to situations where some facilities are overcrowded while others remain underutilized and neglected, resulting in poor maintenance scheduling and budget mismanagement.
1.3 Aim and Objectives of the Study

The primary aim of this research is to design and implement a real-time system for tracking the physical activities of students in a Nigerian university to improve data accuracy, student safety, and administrative decision-making.
To achieve the aforementioned aim, the following specific objectives will be pursued:
To conduct a comprehensive analysis of the existing manual sports tracking methods at the University of Delta and identify their primary weaknesses.
To design a system architecture that utilizes mobile-based GPS and real-time database synchronization to capture student movement data.
To develop a software program (including a mobile-responsive frontend and a robust backend) that processes and visualizes physical activity metrics.
To implement a real-time dashboard for administrators to monitor campus-wide sports participation and identify athletic trends.
The significance of this study is multifaceted, offering benefits to various sectors of the university community:

This system provides a transparent, data-driven basis for the allocation of sports budgets and the scheduling of facility maintenance. It ensures that investments in sports infrastructure are justified by actual usage statistics.
For the Sports Department and Coaches:

It provides an objective tool for talent scouting. By reviewing a student’s digital sports profile, coaches can make informed decisions about who to draft for inter-university competitions like NUGA based on consistent performance rather than a single trial.

It fosters a culture of fitness by allowing students to see their own progress. The gamification of physical activity (through tracking and digital records) can motivate students to stay active, leading to better long-term health outcomes.
In the event of a medical emergency, the system can provide historical data on the student's recent physical exertion, which could be critical for diagnosis and treatment.
For the Field of Computer Science:

This project contributes to the body of knowledge in Mobile Computing and Real-Time Data Processing within a localized African context. It provides a blueprint for other researchers looking to implement IoT-style solutions in environments with fluctuating internet connectivity.
The scope of this research is limited to the development of a real-time tracking application for students at the University of Delta.

The system will focus on tracking outdoor physical activities (such as football, jogging, and track events) where GPS accuracy is most reliable. It will track metrics such as distance covered, duration of activity, and average speed.

The project involves the creation of a mobile interface for students to log activities and a web-based dashboard for administrators. It will utilize existing smartphone sensors rather than custom-built hardware.
The testing and implementation will be confined to the sports facilities and grounds of the University of Delta, Agbor.

2.1.1 The Concept of Real-Time Tracking Systems

In the field of computer science and software engineering, a real-time system is defined as a framework where the validity of the output depends not only on the logical correctness of the computation but also on the temporal window in which that result is delivered (Laplante & Ovaska, 2021). Within the specific domain of physical activity, real-time tracking involves the continuous, high-frequency collection, processing, and visual rendering of spatial, temporal, and physiological data as the athletic event unfolds.

It is essential to distinguish between Hard and Soft real-time systems. While a hard real-time system (such as an aircraft's flight control) cannot tolerate a single millisecond of delay without catastrophic failure, a sports tracking application typically operates as a Soft Real-Time System. In this context, a slight delay or latency in data transmission might degrade the user experience but does not invalidate the entire operation. However, to remain real-time, the system must keep latency to a strict minimum
to ensure that a coach viewing the dashboard in the sports office sees an accurate reflection of the student's current position on the university field.

Sports administration within the Nigerian tertiary education sector has historically been viewed as a peripheral auxiliary service, despite its critical role in student wellness and institutional prestige. The management framework typically follows a top-down hierarchy: a Director of Sports oversees a cadre of specialized coaches, facility managers, and medical personnel. However, as noted by Ekechukwu and Nwachukwu (2022), the operational methodologies
utilized in these departments have remained largely stagnant for decades, relying heavily on manual logbooks, physical registers, and subjective observation.

This analogue approach creates a substantial administrative burden, particularly during high-traffic periods such as the Inter-Faculty Games or preparations for the Nigerian University Games Association (NUGA) tournaments. When hundreds of students converge on the sports complex simultaneously, the manual recording of participation becomes physically impossible for a small coaching staff. Consequently, data regarding training duration, frequency, and intensity is often fragmented, leading to Data Silos where information is trapped in paper files and never analyzed.

Furthermore, the lack of a digital audit trail often leads to Subjective Talent Identification (Ojo & Abiodun, 2023). Without a verifiable, data-backed history of a student’s performance over several semesters, coaches are forced to rely on Trial Day performances, which may not accurately reflect an athlete's true potential or consistency. There is, therefore, a conceptual need to move toward Data-Driven Coaching, where every student has a digital athletic profile that persists throughout their four-year degree at the university.
2.1.3 Location-Based Services (LBS) and GPS in Mobile Computing

To automate the tracking of outdoor physical activities, modern software engineering relies on the integration of Location-Based Services (LBS). LBS is a general term for services that utilize the geographical position of a mobile device to provide specific information or trigger automated actions. The core engine driving LBS in this study is the Global Positioning System (GPS).

GPS functions through a sophisticated constellation of at least 24 satellites orbiting the Earth. These satellites continuously broadcast precise timing and orbital data. A smartphone's GPS receiver picks up these signals and, through a process known as Trilateration, calculates its exact position. By measuring the

it takes for signals from at least four different satellites to reach the device, the receiver can determine its Latitude, Longitude, and Altitude with a high degree of precision (Smith & Jamieson, 2021).

In the specific context of the Agbor campus, the application must account for Signal Noise or Multipath Errors caused by large faculty buildings or dense foliage. To counter this, modern systems often employ Assisted GPS (A-GPS), which utilizes cellular tower data to speed up the
Time to First Fix (TTFF). By polling the GPS chip at synchronized intervals (e.g., every 5 seconds), the tracking system can derive a string of coordinates. By applying mathematical logic
the calculation of distance over time
the system translates these raw coordinates into actionable metrics: current velocity, average pace, and total cumulative distance covered during a sports session.
2.1.4 The Technological Shift: From Wearables to Smartphone Sensors

Historically, the digitalization of athletic tracking was the exclusive domain of proprietary wearable hardware, such as Garmin smartwatches or Fitbit fitness trackers. While these devices provide high-fidelity biometric data, their mass implementation within a Nigerian university setting is hindered by a significant Economic Barrier. The cost of equipping every student-athlete with a high-end wearable is prohibitive, and many students cannot afford to purchase these devices independently (Adeyemo, 2023).

To solve this, there has been a global shift toward Smartphone-Centric Tracking, leveraging the hardware that students already carry. Modern smartphones are equipped with Micro-Electromechanical Systems (MEMS), which include the accelerometer, gyroscope, and magnetometer.
The Accelerometer: Measures the non-gravitational acceleration of the device. This allows the software to detect Step Counts and sudden bursts of explosive movement during a sprint.

The Gyroscope: Measures the orientation and angular velocity. This helps the system understand the tilt of the body, which is essential for distinguishing between different types of movement (e.g., running vs. cycling).
the process of combining GPS data with MEMS sensor data

the application can provide a more accurate picture of physical activity than GPS alone. For example, if a student is running under a covered pavilion where GPS signals are weak, the accelerometer can continue to track steps and movement, ensuring that the athletic data remains consistent. This Hardware-Agnostic approach is the most sustainable model for Nigerian universities, as it relies on the students' existing mobile infrastructure to deliver high-end tracking capabilities.

The structural integrity of this research is supported by a dual-layered theoretical framework. This framework addresses both the technical backbone of the software (the Client-Server Model) and the psychological factors governing its adoption by the student body (the Technology Acceptance Model).

The technical foundation of this project is anchored in the Client-Server Architecture, a distributed application structure that partitions tasks between the providers of a resource (the server) and the service requesters (the clients). Within the specific context of this sports tracking system, the architecture follows an N-tier approach to ensure modularity and scalability.

The student’s mobile application functions as a Thick Client. This means that the application does not merely act as a display; it carries a significant portion of the computational load at the edge of the network. The client is responsible for interfacing directly with the smartphone’s hardware abstraction layer to poll GPS and MEMS sensors. Critically, it performs Edge Validation

a process where the application filters out erroneous coordinate spikes caused by signal interference from large buildings on the UNIDEL campus before the data is transmitted. By handling this logic locally, the system reduces the volume of redundant data sent over the network, which is vital in an environment where mobile data costs and network stability are significant concerns.

Conversely, the server acts as the Central Intelligence Hub. Whether hosted on a local university server or a cloud platform, the server is tasked with managing the Session State of hundreds of concurrent student-athletes. It receives the asynchronous streams of JSON data, parses the geographical coordinates, and performs the heavy mathematical lifting

such as calculating cumulative distance and average velocity. This separation of concerns ensures that the energy-intensive data analytics are handled by a machine with a constant power supply, thereby preserving the battery life of the students' mobile devices (Kurose & Ross, 2021).

From a socio-technical and user-adoption perspective, the design of the interface is strictly guided by the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) originally proposed by Davis (1989). TAM is the industry standard for predicting whether a new technology will be embraced or rejected by its target demographic. The model posits that two primary Cognitive Determinants dictate the behavioral intention to use a system: Perceived Usefulness (PU) and Perceived Ease of Use (PEOU).

For the students at the University of Delta, PEOU is addressed through a Zero-Friction interface design. The tracking process must be initiated within two screen taps; any complexity beyond this would lead to System Fatigue, where students simply stop using the app. Furthermore, the application must demonstrate low Resource Consumption. If a student perceives that the app is the primary cause of battery drain during a 45-minute football match, the PEOU rating will plummet, leading to high abandonment rates regardless of administrative mandates.
Perceived Usefulness (PU) is addressed by moving the app beyond a mere monitoring tool and into a fitness companion. By providing the student with immediate, high-fidelity visual feedback
such as an interactive map of their running route and a breakdown of their personal bests
the system provides an intrinsic reward. This transforms the app from a university-imposed obligation into a valuable personal asset, ensuring long-term engagement and data accuracy.

A critical analysis of contemporary literature reveals a significant evolution in how physical activity is monitored in academic settings. However, each existing methodology presents localized failures that this project seeks to rectify.

Biometric Attendance Systems (Bello & Nnamdi, 2021): Bello and Nnamdi (2021) implemented a fingerprint-based biometric system to curb absenteeism in mandatory physical education classes at a Nigerian federal university. Their study celebrated a 94% reduction in proxy signing.
While effective for verifying presence, this system is binary and static. It confirms
a student entered the sports complex but offers zero insight into
they did inside. A student could theoretically scan their finger and sit idly on the

bleachers. The proposed real-time tracking system renders this model obsolete by shifting the focus from attendance to active participation, providing granular data on the intensity and duration of the exertion.

Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) Beacons (Johansson & Lindberg, 2022): In a European university context, Johansson and Lindberg (2022) deployed a network of weather-proof BLE beacons around campus athletics tracks to log movement.

While technically sophisticated and ideal for indoor dead zones where GPS is weak, this model is economically and logistically unviable for the University of Delta. The capital expenditure required to install and maintain hundreds of powered beacons across the Agbor campus would be prohibitive. Furthermore, in the Nigerian context, such external hardware is highly susceptible to vandalism, theft, and power outages. My research pivots away from External Hardware Dependence toward Sensor Ubiquity, using the hardware already in the students' pockets.

Self-Reporting Mobile Applications (Oladipo et al., 2023): Oladipo et al. (2023) designed a cardiovascular health app for amateur athletes in Lagos, which relied on users manually inputting their training duration and perceived intensity.

The fatal flaw of this system was subjectivity and human error. The researchers noted a staggering 30% discrepancy between reported and actual activity. Students often overestimate their exertion or simply forget to log their sessions. This highlights the absolute necessity for Automation. By removing the human in the loop and allowing GPS to record data autonomously, my project ensures that the sports directorate receives objective, unvarnished performance data.

Theoretical IoT Frameworks (Chukwuma & Alabi, 2024): Chukwuma and Alabi (2024) recently proposed a comprehensive Smart Sports portal for African universities, theoretically integrating GPS, RFID, and cloud scheduling.

This work remains purely conceptual. While it correctly identifies the problem of Network Latency in developing nations, it offers no programmatic solution. My research builds upon this theoretical foundation by moving into the Implementation Phase, specifically developing a Local Caching Algorithm that allows the app to store
tracking data when the network (MTN/Airtel) fails and synchronize it once the signal is restored.
2.4 Summary of Literature and Research Gap

The exhaustive review of the existing body of knowledge reveals a clear, three-stage evolutionary trajectory in the domain of sports management technology. This progression has moved from the Analogue Era of manual paper-based registers and stopwatches, to the First Digital Wave of static biometric entry logs (fingerprint/RFID), and eventually to the contemporary IoT Revolution involving high-precision wearable telemetry. However, while the global landscape has embraced these advancements, a multi-dimensional gap persists
particularly concerning the deployment of these technologies within the specific socio-technical environment of Nigerian universities.

The literature synthesized in this chapter underscores a fundamental shift in the philosophy of athletic monitoring. Research indicates that Presence (knowing a student is at the field) is no longer sufficient for modern sports administration; Performance (knowing what the student is doing in real-time) is the new gold standard.

The conceptual review established that Global Positioning Systems (GPS) and MEMS sensors have become democratized through the ubiquity of smartphones, offering a viable alternative to expensive specialized hardware. The theoretical framework, grounded in the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), highlighted that for any tracking system to succeed in a university setting, it must prioritize Perceived Ease of Use to ensure student compliance. Finally, the empirical review of previous works in Nigeria and abroad demonstrated that while we have solved the problem of
identifying participants, we have yet to solve the problem of tracking them dynamically in an environment characterized by fluctuating network connectivity and economic constraints.

More importantly, this project introduces a programmatic solution to the Connectivity Problem. Unlike previous systems that crash or lose data during network timeouts, this system implements an

By delivering a functional, real-time tracking program tailored for the University of Delta, this research moves the discourse from conceptual speculation to tangible software implementation.

System analysis is the systematic process of investigating a complex operational environment, identifying its inherent inefficiencies, and defining the specific requirements for a superior technological replacement. It serves as the foundational phase of the software development lifecycle, ensuring that the transition from a conceptual hypothesis to a deployable digital solution is governed by logic rather than intuition. In the context of the Real-Time Student Physical Activity Tracking System, system analysis provides the architectural blueprint required to bridge the gap between physical athletic exertion and administrative record-keeping at the University of Delta (UNIDEL), Agbor.

The primary objective of this chapter is to provide a rigorous deconstruction of the current manual sports management workflows and present a comprehensive design for an automated, sensor-driven alternative. It moves beyond the theoretical literature established in Chapter Two to address the concrete engineering challenges of real-time telemetry, such as managing high-velocity data streams and ensuring system resilience during network fluctuations.

This chapter follows a structured analytical sequence: it defines the Object-Oriented Analysis and Design (OOAD) methodology; performs a critical evaluation of the existing paper-based registry; and details the structural, database, and interface designs of the proposed system. By adhering to this formal analytical framework, the study ensures that the resulting software is not merely a collection of disparate code fragments but a cohesive, scalable, and reliable tool capable of
sports administration within the unique infrastructural landscape of a Nigerian university.
The methodology adopted for the architectural

and development of this project is the Object-Oriented Analysis and Design (OOAD) framework. OOAD is a technical approach that models a complex system as a collection of discrete, interacting objects, each possessing

(functions). Unlike traditional procedural programming, which focuses on a linear sequence of tasks, OOAD focuses on the entities that make up the system, making it the ideal choice for a modular, real-time tracking application.
The selection of OOAD for this research is predicated on several critical engineering requirements:
Mapping Physical Entities to Digital Objects: In the context of the University of Delta sports ecosystem, physical entities such as a Student a Coach
and a Sporting Facility are directly mapped to software objects. For instance, a Student Object encapsulates specific attributes like
Abstraction and Encapsulation: OOAD allows for the complexity of the smartphone's hardware
specifically the GPS and accelerometer sensors

to be abstracted. The application logic interacts with a simplified Location Service object without needing to manage the low-level satellite handshakes, thereby reducing the risk of bugs during the implementation phase.

System Scalability (Inheritance): By defining a base class for Physical Activity, the system can easily be extended through inheritance to support specific sports. For example, a Football Session and a Track Sprint can both inherit core distance-tracking logic while adding unique metrics relevant to their specific sport type.

The methodology is executed in two distinct phases: Object-Oriented Analysis (OOA), which focuses on identifying the what (the requirements and objects), and Object-Oriented Design (OOD), which focuses on the how (the logical architecture and class interactions).

The current operational framework for managing student athletic participation at the University of Delta (UNIDEL), Agbor, is entirely analogue and manual. The system is comprised of physical ledgers and attendance registers held within the Sports Directorate. This manual workflow is the primary mechanism for verifying student presence at trials, departmental sports weeks, and personal fitness sessions required for certain academic credits.
Under the existing system, the workflow follows a strictly linear and physical path:
Manual Check-in: Upon arrival at the university sports complex or football pitch, a student must locate the presiding official or coach.

Ledger Entry: The student is required to manually enter their details into a paper-based logbook. The fields typically include the date, name, matriculation number, department, and the specific sport to be undertaken.

Time-Stamping: The Start Time and End Time are recorded based on the official's wristwatch or the student's estimation, both of which are prone to significant human error and rounding inconsistencies.
Physical Storage: At the conclusion of the sporting day, these paper registers are gathered and stored in physical filing cabinets within the Sports Directorate offices.

This system is inherently static. The data remains trapped on paper, inaccessible to other university departments (such as the Medical Unit or the Student Affairs Office) unless the physical book is transported between offices. There is no mechanism for verifying that a student who signed the book actually participated in the activity, as the system lacks any form of spatial or physiological validation. Consequently, the existing system is a post-event record-keeping tool rather than a real-time management system.

The proposed system is an automated, high-fidelity tracking architecture designed to replace the subjectivity of manual record-keeping with the objectivity of sensor-driven telemetry. Unlike the existing analogue framework, this solution functions as a Passive Observer, utilizing the pervasive nature of modern smartphone technology to record student exertion without requiring constant user intervention.

The core of the proposed system lies in its ability to transform raw satellite signals into actionable athletic intelligence. By interfacing directly with the device's Global Positioning System (GPS) and tri-axial accelerometer, the software establishes a persistent Digital Breadcrumb trail. These data points

The Controller: Serving as the intermediary, the Controller listens to events from the View (such as a Start Tracking button click) and triggers the corresponding logic in the Model. It also manages the polling frequency of the GPS hardware and handles the routing of data to the backend server.

To objectively determine the efficacy and reliability of the tracking system within the UNIDEL environment, the following metrics will be monitored and documented during the implementation and testing phase (Chapter Four).
This metric evaluates the fidelity of the GPS data. It is measured as the horizontal distance (in
) between the coordinate reported by the smartphone and the student's actual physical position on the pitch. The goal is to achieve a Circular Error Probable (CEP) of less than 5
. This is critical because excessive GPS drift can lead to inflated distance calculations, falsely suggesting a student ran further or faster than they actually did.
Latency refers to the temporal delay between the physical occurrence of a movement and its visual representation on the administrator’s screen. This metric is composed of three parts:
Polling Latency: The 5-second interval between sensor captures.
Transit Latency: The time taken for the data packet to travel across the mobile network (MTN/Airtel/Glo) to the server.
Processing Latency: The time the server takes to compute the results. The target for a Real-Time experience is an end-to-end latency of under 10 seconds.

Given the potential for network outages on campus, Sync Reliability measures the percentage of data points successfully recovered from the local cache. If a student loses their internet signal for 10 minutes, the system should have cached approximately 120 points (at a 5-second interval). Reliability is 100% if all 120 points are successfully uploaded to the central server once the signal returns. Any loss in this Store-and-Forward mechanism would result in gaps in the student's athletic trail, rendering the session data incomplete.

4.4 Core Algorithmic Implementation: The Haversine Formula

A fundamental engineering challenge in developing a real-time tracking system is the accurate translation of raw geographical coordinates (Latitude and Longitude) provided by the mobile device into a measurable physical distance (

). Conventional Euclidean geometry is insufficient for this task because the Earth is an oblate spheroid rather than a flat plane. To account for the Earth's curvature, this research adopts the Haversine Formula within the Python-based backend.

The Haversine formula is a spherical trigonometric equation that determines the Great-Circle Distance between two points on a sphere. By calculating the central angle between two sets of coordinates, the system can determine the exact displacement of a student-athlete between any two 5-second polling intervals.

This research set out to address a specific administrative and health-related gap within the Nigerian university ecosystem: the lack of an automated, real-time mechanism for tracking student physical activities. Through the course of this study, we have moved from the conceptualization of the problem to the full implementation of a software solution.

In Chapter One, we established that the manual recording of sports activities at the University of Delta was inefficient and prone to data integrity issues. Chapter Two provided a comprehensive review of existing literature, highlighting the shift from expensive wearable hardware to the use of ubiquitous smartphone sensors. Chapter Three detailed the Object-Oriented Analysis and Design (OOAD) methodology, providing the architectural blueprints for the system. Finally, Chapter Four documented the actual construction of the application using Python and VS Code, demonstrating how the Haversine formula and offline caching mechanisms solve the real-world problems of geographical distance calculation and network instability.

The developed system successfully allows students to log their sporting sessions via a mobile-responsive interface, while providing university administrators with a live, map-based dashboard to monitor participation and safety. By digitizing this process, the university can now move toward a more objective, data-driven approach to sports management and talent identification.

The Development of a Real-Time System for Tracking Students Physical Activities (Sports) in Nigeria University demonstrates that sophisticated technological solutions do not always require expensive, imported hardware. By leveraging the sensors already present in students' mobile devices and utilizing robust backend logic, we have created a system that is both economically viable and technically sound for the local environment.

The successful implementation of this project proves that real-time data processing can significantly enhance the safety and accountability of campus sports. It moves the University of Delta away from archaic paper-based logs and toward a Smart Campus model. Ultimately, this system serves as a bridge between physical health and digital informatics, ensuring that every drop of sweat on the track is accounted for in the university’s digital records.
Based on the findings and the implementation experience of this project, the following recommendations are made to ensure the sustainability and growth of the system:

The University Sports Directorate should officially adopt the system for all inter-faculty and inter-departmental competitions. This will ensure a steady stream of data and encourage student participation in the digital ecosystem.

To minimize the impact of network latency, the university should consider providing dedicated Wi-Fi hotspots at major sporting venues, such as the football pitch and the gymnasium, to ensure seamless real-time data synchronization.

The university could introduce a Fitness Leaderboard where students with the highest verified activity levels receive digital certificates or small academic incentives. This would drive user adoption based on the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) principles discussed in Chapter Two.

While the current system relies on smartphones, future iterations could include low-cost NFC (Near Field Communication) tags at facility entrances to provide a secondary layer of location verification.
While this project provides a solid foundation for real-time tracking, there is room for further research and expansion:

Future researchers could explore integrating the system with low-cost heart rate monitors or smartwatches to provide physiological data (e.g., heart rate, calories burned) alongside the current spatial data (distance, speed).
By applying Machine Learning (ML) algorithms to the historical data collected by this system, future studies could develop models to predict student injury risks based on training patterns.
Research into utilizing Wi-Fi Fingerprinting or Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) beacons could expand the tracking capabilities to indoor facilities where GPS signals are traditionally weak.
